chunks: Over/undervoltage on an embedded system. The question: What happens if you get an over/undervoltage on an embedded system?
When a microcontroller's supply leaves its allowed range, two different things happen.
Too low a voltage causes malfunction: logic slows down, the processor can run garbage, and a write to flash (the memory that keeps settings) can be cut halfway.
Too high a voltage causes damage: thin insulating layers inside the chip break down, and a pin pushed above the supply can trigger latch-up.
So you add a brown-out reset, a supervisor, series resistors and clamps on inputs, correct power-up order, and firmware guards.
Think of a cook at a stove. With too little heat the food is only half cooked, and nothing looks burnt, but the meal is wrong.
That is undervoltage: the chip still runs, but badly. With far too much heat the pan burns and cracks: overvoltage damage.
A good cook stops cooking if the gas pressure drops too low (brown-out reset). The analogy leaves out one hazard: a pin driven while the chip is off partly powers it.
A 1. 1 volts dip from 3. 3 volts (down to about 2. 2 volts) crosses the 2. 7 volts BOR threshold, so the chip is reset cleanly rather than running in the marginal band.
Without BOR (or with the threshold set at 1. 8 volts) the chip would run through the dip at reduced margins.
The numbers are examples: BOR levels and minimum operating voltages are device-specific.
Brown-out reset (BOR): holds the chip in reset while the supply is below a threshold. Supervisor: an external chip that monitors the rail and releases reset after a delay.
Clamp diodes: protective diodes on each pin that conduct if the pin goes above the supply or below ground.
Latch-up: an unintended structure inside the chip that switches on and shorts the supply until power is removed.
Back-powering: powering a chip through a pin's clamp diode while its supply is off.
A 3. 3 volts microcontroller has a BOR threshold of 2. 7 volts. If the rail dips to 2. 2 volts for a moment, the chip is reset cleanly instead of running in the unreliable band.
Now an exposed input: a 12 volts signal feeds a pin that clamps near 3. 6 volts. A 1 kilohms series resistor limits the clamp current to (12 minus 3. 6) over 1000 equals 8.
4 milliamps, which the diodes can survive. That is the whole idea.
"Undervoltage makes the system misbehave: slower logic, corrupted RAM, half-written flash, weak I/O, so you add brown-out reset and a supervisor.
Overvoltage damages it: breakdown above the absolute maximum, and a pin above Vdd forward-biases the ESD diodes and can trigger latch-up.

So I use brown-out detection, series resistors and clamps on exposed inputs, proper power sequencing, and a fuse or OVP on the rail, plus firmware that resets on brown-out and avoids flash writes when the supply is weak."
